sketchNote: The whole sheet goes to the scrum: a dozen figures worked into one another over the cobblestones, the buildings behind them barely roughed in. Through the center runs one taut line — hauling Charles forward — and every hand in the drawing is fighting for it.

map.address: Riverfront at the end of Madison Street

history: The crowd pulled Charles away from the authorities and brought him down to the riverbank, where he boarded a waiting skiff.
He crossed to West Troy — now Watervliet — and was briefly taken again on landing, before his allies secured his freedom for good.

scenes.label: River Escape

quote.text: The crowd was like a lynch mob in reverse.
quote.source: Freeing Charles: The Struggle to Free a Slave on the Eve of the Civil War, p. 113

paragraphs: Behind Charles, the mob and his captors surged through the streets of Troy, pressing toward the Washington Street Ferry Landing. Finally, the distance between Charles and freedom felt reachable, but fate had other plans. Ahead, Charles could see the ferry departing; the old wood planks beneath his feet seemed to creak with the weight of his despair as he watched the ferry float upriver, leaving only a trail of churning water in its wake—another reminder that freedom was fleeting and didn’t come easily or without a fight.

Bound and shackled, standing at the edge of the Hudson, Charles could feel his options thinning and the desperation of the moment growing. Marshal Holmes and the slave catchers were closing in fast, the sound of their footfalls growing louder with each passing second. By now, the trail of churning water from the ferry had disappeared and, seemingly, along with it, the path to freedom.

Then, in a quick-thinking rescue effort, local waterman Billy Loreman, with the help of willing hands, pulled a still-bound Charles aboard a small skiff, his oars cutting through the water with practiced precision in an all-out effort for the far shore. From the landing behind them, the dumbfounded shouting of Marshal Holmes and the slave catchers grew quieter.

Behind him, the rage-filled faces of Marshal Holmes and the slave catchers radiated enough heat to dry up the Hudson. Across the river in West Troy (modern-day Watervliet), freedom lay just feet away—freedom that vanished no slower than the time it took Billy Loreman to secure the skiff. From an eyeshot’s distance, Charles could see the local West Troy police strutting toward him in a pompous march, ready to rip the taste of freedom from his mouth and send shockwaves through the Troy abolitionist community.

historicalContext: At the height of the Underground Railroad, the Hudson River had up to 500 ships moving upstream a day, many with black captains, making it an efficient escape route, transporting freedom-seekers from New York City to Canada in just one week—far faster than the more dangerous overland routes.

After Charles crossed the river into West Troy and was taken into custody by Albany County sheriff’s deputies and federal postmaster, Harriet Tubman and several hundred citizens crossed the river and surrounded the justice’s office at Corporation Hall Building, where Charles was being held.

In 1790, throughout the Hudson Valley—the region along both sides of the Hudson River from Yonkers to Albany—the first federal census counted more than 21,000 enslaved New Yorkers, nearly as many as documented in the State of Georgia, which had 29,264. By 1860, when Charles Nalle escaped, Georgia had as many as 462,198 enslaved people.

morals.title:
AUTHORITARIANISM
IS PERSISTENT
morals.message: Marshal Holmes and the slave catchers represent authoritarian forces suppressing freedom—a challenge that continues today through power-seeking individuals and politicians who favor and enforce strict obedience to governmental authority.

callToAction.title: It comes back
callToAction.content: Stand up against authoritarian laws & leaders by staying informed, voting, protesting, using your voice & the press to promote democratic values & hold leaders accountable.
